name: P2 · Unit 5 DBMS — 1. Concepts & Architecture (180 Q)
description: Database System Concepts and Architecture: data models; schemas and instances; three-schema architecture; data independence; database languages and interfaces; centralized and client/server architectures. 30 questions per sub-topic.

questions.question: A data model is best defined as:

options.A: The physical file layout of a database on disk
options.B: A diagram of the network connecting clients to the server
options.C: A set of sample records used for testing
options.D: A collection of concepts to describe the structure of a database (data types, relationships, constraints) together with basic operations on it

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: A data model describes structure (types, relationships, constraints) and usually a set of basic operations for retrievals and updates.

questions.question: Which data model is classified as a high-level (conceptual) data model?
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Conceptual models such as the ER model use concepts close to how users perceive data (entities, attributes, relationships).

questions.question: Representational (implementation) data models include:

options.A: ER model and UML class diagrams

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Representational models are understood by end users yet close to how data is organised in storage; the relational, network and hierarchical models are the classic ones.

questions.question: Physical (low-level) data models describe:

options.B: Record formats, record orderings and access paths on the storage medium
options.C: Only the external views of users

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Physical data models describe how data is stored as files: record formats, orderings and access paths.

questions.question: In database terminology, an 'access path' is:

options.A: A search structure, such as an index, that makes locating particular records efficient
options.B: The login path of a user
options.C: A network route between client and server
options.D: The directory in which database files are stored

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: An access path (e.g. an index) speeds up searching for records that satisfy a condition.

questions.question: In the hierarchical data model, data are organised as:

options.A: A general graph with many-to-many links
options.C: A tree structure in which each child record has exactly one parent

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: The hierarchical model uses parent–child (1:N) relationships arranged as trees.

questions.question: IBM's IMS (Information Management System) is based on the:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: IMS, developed in the 1960s, is the best-known hierarchical DBMS; it uses the DL/I language.

questions.question: How are many-to-many relationships handled in a pure hierarchical model?

options.B: They cannot be stored at all
options.D: By duplicating records or using virtual (logical) parent–child relationships

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Since each child has one parent, M:N relationships lead to duplicated records unless virtual/logical pointers are used, which is a key weakness.

questions.question: The network data model was standardised by the:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: The CODASYL DBTG report (1971) defined the network model; IDMS is a well-known implementation.

questions.question: In the CODASYL network model, a 1:N relationship between record types is represented by a:

options.C: Set type with an owner record type and a member record type

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: A set type links one owner record to many member records; M:N needs an intermediate (link) record type.

questions.question: Which DBMS is based on the network model?
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: IDMS (Integrated Database Management System) follows the CODASYL network model; IMS is hierarchical.

questions.question: E. F. Codd proposed the relational model in 1970 in the paper titled:

options.A: The Entity–Relationship Model: Toward a Unified View of Data
options.C: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
options.D: Relational Completeness of Data Base Sublanguages

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Codd's 1970 CACM paper introduced the relational model; Chen's 1976 paper introduced the ER model.

questions.question: The formal foundation of the relational model is:

options.B: Set theory and first-order predicate logic

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Relations are sets of tuples, and relational algebra/calculus are based on set theory and first-order logic.

questions.question: 'Record-at-a-time', navigational data manipulation is characteristic of:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Legacy models navigate from record to record using pointers (e.g. DL/I, CODASYL DML); SQL is set-at-a-time.

questions.question: The Entity–Relationship model was proposed by:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Peter P. Chen introduced the ER model in 1976; Bachman is known for the network model and Bachman diagrams.

questions.question: Codd's well-known rules for judging a relational DBMS (1985) consist of:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: They are called the '12 rules' but are numbered 0 (the foundation rule) to 12, i.e. 13 rules.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a record-based data model?
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: The ER model is a conceptual (object-based) model; the other three structure the database as fixed-format records.

questions.question: In a self-describing data model such as XML or many NoSQL systems:

options.A: Data must be in first normal form
options.B: The schema is stored only in a separate catalog
options.C: The description of the data is stored together with the data values

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Self-describing models combine data and its description, e.g. XML tags or JSON keys.

questions.question: MongoDB is an example of which type of NoSQL data model?
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: MongoDB stores JSON-like (BSON) documents, which can have nested structures.

questions.question: Apache Cassandra and HBase are examples of:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: They organise data into column families, inspired by Google's Bigtable.

questions.question: Neo4j stores data as nodes and relationships (edges) with properties. It is a:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Neo4j implements the property-graph data model.

questions.question: A pure key–value store (for example Redis or Amazon DynamoDB in its basic form) accesses data mainly by:

options.C: A unique key, with the value largely opaque to the system

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Key–value stores give very fast lookups by key; the system usually does not interpret the value's structure.

questions.question: Which feature is characteristic of the object data model?

options.A: Data are organised only as trees
options.B: Relationships are stored only as foreign keys
options.D: Each object has a system-generated object identity (OID) independent of its attribute values

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: OIDs are immutable and unique; object models also support encapsulation, classes and inheritance.

questions.question: The object–relational data model:

options.A: Extends the relational model with features such as user-defined types, inheritance and complex objects

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Object–relational features were standardised in SQL:1999 (and later), e.g. in Oracle and PostgreSQL.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A data model specifies both the structure of a database and operations on it.
II. Physical data models are mainly intended for end users.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Physical models are for computer specialists, not end users; statement I is correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The relational model offers better data independence than the network model.
Reason (R): In the relational model, relationships are represented by data values (keys) rather than by physical pointers.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Because relationships are value-based, storage structures can change without affecting how relationships are expressed.

questions.question: In the relational model, a relationship between two relations is represented by:

options.A: Matching values of attributes, typically a foreign key referring to a primary key

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Relational databases connect tables through values, e.g. EMPLOYEE.Dno referencing DEPARTMENT.Dnumber.

questions.question: In the object data model, the behaviour (dynamic aspect) of objects is specified through:
questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: Object models bundle data with operations (methods); users invoke operations instead of accessing data directly.

questions.question: Which statement about the pure hierarchical model is FALSE?

options.A: Access usually begins at the root and navigates downwards
options.B: Each record type except the root has exactly one parent record type
options.D: A child record can have several parent records

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: In a pure hierarchy a child has only one parent, which is why M:N relationships are hard to model.

questions.question: Conceptual data models such as the ER model are mainly used during:

options.C: Conceptual database design, independent of any specific DBMS

questions.subject: Data Models
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema is later mapped to a representational model (e.g. relational) during logical design.

questions.question: The description of a database, specified during database design and not expected to change frequently, is called the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The schema describes the structure; the data stored at any moment is the state (instance).

questions.question: The data in a database at a particular moment in time is called the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Every insert, delete or update produces a new database state.

questions.question: The schema and the database state are also called, respectively, the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Schema = intension; database state = extension of the schema.

questions.question: When a new database is defined but no data has yet been loaded, it is in the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Specifying the schema to the DBMS creates an empty database; loading data then gives the initial state.

questions.question: The state of a database when it is first populated (loaded) with data is called the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: After defining the schema, the first loading of data produces the initial database state.

questions.question: A database state that satisfies the structure and all the constraints specified in the schema is called a:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Every state should be valid; the DBMS enforces the constraints.

questions.question: Who is primarily responsible for ensuring that every state of the database is a valid state?

options.C: The DBMS, by enforcing the constraints defined in the schema

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The DBMS checks constraints such as keys, domains and referential integrity on each update.

questions.question: In a DBMS, the database schema (meta-data) is stored in the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The catalog stores the schema so the DBMS and its users can refer to it; this is the self-describing nature of databases.

questions.question: Which of the following is typically NOT shown in a schema diagram?

options.C: Actual data values of the records

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: A schema diagram shows only aspects of the schema; data values belong to the database state.

questions.question: Each object within a schema, such as STUDENT or COURSE, is called a:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Record types, data items and constraints in a schema are schema constructs.

questions.question: Adding a new attribute such as Date_of_birth to the STUDENT record type after the database is in use is an example of:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Changes to the schema after the database is operational are called schema evolution; modern DBMSs allow some changes without reloading.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?

options.A: The schema changes with every insertion
options.B: The database state changes frequently, while the schema changes rarely

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Every update changes the state; the schema changes only when requirements change.

questions.question: For a relation schema R(A1, A2, …, An), n is called the:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The degree is the number of attributes in the relation schema.

questions.question: The number of tuples in a relation state r(R) is called its:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Cardinality = number of tuples; degree = number of attributes.

questions.question: A STUDENT relation has 6 attributes and currently holds 250 tuples. Its degree and cardinality are:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Degree counts attributes (6) and cardinality counts tuples (250).

questions.question: Formally, a relation state r(R) of R(A1, …, An) is a subset of:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: A relation state is a subset of the Cartesian product of the attribute domains.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B) has |dom(A)| = 3 and |dom(B)| = 4. How many different relation states r(R) are possible?
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: There are 3 × 4 = 12 possible tuples, and any subset of them is a possible state, so 2^12 = 4096 states.

questions.question: Which statement about tuples in a relation is correct?

options.A: The ordering of tuples in a relation is not significant
options.B: Tuples must be sorted by the primary key
options.D: Tuples are stored and must be retrieved in insertion order

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: A relation is a set of tuples, so there is no inherent order and no duplicate tuples.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The order of tuples in a relation is not significant.
II. If a tuple is defined as an ordered list of values, the order of values within a tuple matters.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Both are correct; with the alternative definition as a set of (attribute, value) pairs, attribute order also becomes irrelevant.

questions.question: A relation that currently contains no tuples is:

options.B: Not allowed by the relational model
options.C: A valid relation state (an empty relation)

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: An empty set of tuples is a legitimate relation state.

questions.question: Which SQL statement changes the database schema rather than only the database state?

options.D: ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Email VARCHAR(40)

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: ALTER TABLE is a DDL statement that modifies the schema; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change only the state.

questions.question: In a programming-language analogy, a database schema corresponds to a:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The schema is like a type (the structure); the state is like the current value of a variable of that type.

questions.question: 'Meta-data' in a database system means:

options.D: Data about data, such as the definitions of tables, columns and constraints

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Meta-data describes the structure of the database and is stored in the catalog.

questions.question: The term 'snapshot' in database terminology usually refers to:

options.C: The database state at a particular moment

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: Database state, instance, occurrence and snapshot all mean the data at a particular time.

questions.question: A constraint that must hold on every individual database state (for example, 'Ssn is unique') is called a:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: State constraints restrict each valid state; transition constraints restrict how the database may change from one state to another.

questions.question: 'An employee's salary can never decrease' is an example of a:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: It restricts the change from one state to the next, so it is a transition constraint, usually enforced with triggers or application code.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The schema of a relation can remain the same while its state changes many times per second.
Reason (R): The schema is the intension, while the state is the extension of the database.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The intension (structure) is stable; the extension (actual tuples) changes with every update.

questions.question: Loading a large amount of existing data into a newly defined database to create its first state is typically done using:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: DBMS loading utilities load existing files efficiently into the database to create the initial state.

questions.question: In the SQL standard, schema information about tables and columns can be queried through the set of views called:
questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: The standard INFORMATION_SCHEMA views expose catalog information such as TABLES and COLUMNS.

questions.question: The SQL statement  CREATE SCHEMA COMPANY AUTHORIZATION 'Jsmith';  does what?

options.A: Grants Jsmith access to all schemas
options.B: Creates a schema named COMPANY owned by the user Jsmith

questions.subject: Schemas and Instances
questions.explanation: An SQL schema groups tables and other elements belonging to one application; AUTHORIZATION names its owner.

questions.question: The three-schema architecture of a DBMS was proposed by the:

options.A: ANSI/SPARC Study Group on Database Management Systems

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The ANSI/SPARC architecture (1975–78) introduced the external, conceptual and internal levels.

questions.question: The main goal of the three-schema architecture is to:

options.B: Separate user applications from the physical database

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Separating the levels supports multiple user views and data independence.

questions.question: The three levels of the ANSI/SPARC architecture, from the user side to the storage side, are:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: External level (user views), conceptual level (whole database) and internal level (physical storage).

questions.question: Which level describes the physical storage structures and access paths of the database?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The internal schema uses a physical data model to describe storage details.

questions.question: Which level describes the structure of the whole database for a community of users, hiding physical storage details?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema describes entities, data types, relationships, user operations and constraints for the entire database.

questions.question: Which level describes the part of the database that a particular user group is interested in?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Each external schema (user view) hides the rest of the database from that group.

questions.question: An index created on EMPLOYEE(Salary) to speed up queries is described at the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Indexes are access paths, which belong to the internal schema.

questions.question: A view that shows only student names and roll numbers to the library staff belongs to the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: User views that hide other data are external schemas.

questions.question: The definition 'DEPARTMENT(Dnumber, Dname, Mgr_ssn) with Dnumber as the primary key' is part of the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Relations, attributes and constraints for the whole database are defined in the conceptual schema.

questions.question: For a single database in the three-schema architecture, how many schemas of each kind exist?

options.A: One external, many conceptual, one internal
options.C: Many external, one conceptual, one internal

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: There are many user views but only one conceptual and one internal schema for a database.

questions.question: The processes of transforming requests and results between the levels of the three-schema architecture are called:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: External/conceptual and conceptual/internal mappings translate requests downward and results upward.

questions.question: The two mappings defined in the three-schema architecture are:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Each external schema maps to the conceptual schema, which maps to the internal schema.

questions.question: A disadvantage of a strict three-schema implementation is:

options.C: The overhead of transforming requests and results between levels at run time

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Mapping between levels takes time; many DBMSs therefore do not separate the levels completely.

questions.question: When implementing the three-schema architecture, the conceptual schema is usually described using:

options.B: A representational (implementation) data model, such as the relational model

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: In practice the conceptual schema is expressed in the DBMS's implementation data model, often derived from a high-level ER design.

questions.question: In relational DBMSs, external schemas are mainly implemented using:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: SQL views present derived, restricted pictures of the base tables to different users.

questions.question: Record placement, file organisation, compression and encryption of stored data are concerns of the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: These are physical storage details described in the internal schema.

questions.question: In the three-schema architecture, a query written against an external schema is processed by:

options.B: Sending it to every external schema
options.D: Transforming it into a request on the conceptual schema and then into a request on the internal schema

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The DBMS maps the request level by level down to the stored database, and maps results back up.

questions.question: Which statement about the three-schema architecture is correct?

options.A: It removes the need for a catalog
options.B: Most DBMSs support the architecture to some extent but do not separate the levels completely
options.C: All commercial DBMSs separate the three levels strictly
options.D: It applies only to hierarchical databases

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Many DBMSs mix conceptual and internal details in their DDL, although they support user views.

questions.question: The schemas at all three levels are stored as meta-data in the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The catalog keeps the external, conceptual and internal schemas and the mappings between them.

questions.question: Who is mainly responsible for defining the internal schema?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The DBA handles physical design decisions such as indexes and storage organisation.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A user view may include data derived from stored data that is not physically stored.
II. Different external schemas may present the same data differently.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Views can contain derived attributes (e.g. age from date of birth) and each user group can see its own representation.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The three-schema architecture makes it possible to provide multiple user views of the same database.
Reason (R): The conceptual schema describes the whole database, from which each external schema is derived through a mapping.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Because every view is defined from the common conceptual schema, many different views can coexist.

questions.question: The stored database on disk is described directly by the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The internal schema describes the physical storage of the database.

questions.question: Which of the following changes is made at the conceptual level?

options.C: Adding a new entity type PROJECT with its attributes

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: New entity types, attributes and relationships change the conceptual schema; the other options are internal-level changes.

questions.question: Which user is most likely to interact only with an external schema?

options.D: A bank teller using a banking application

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: End users see only the part of the database relevant to them through their application's view.

questions.question: In the ANSI/SPARC architecture, security is enhanced because:

options.B: Each user can be restricted to their own external schema, hiding other data

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Views hide data that a user group is not allowed to see.

questions.question: A single conceptual schema supporting many external schemas mainly helps to:

options.D: Integrate data in one place while serving diverse user requirements

questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Data are integrated and stored once, while different users get customised views.

questions.question: If only the internal schema changes (for example, a file is reorganised), what else must be changed?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: Only the mapping between the conceptual and internal levels is updated; this is physical data independence.

questions.question: In the three-schema architecture, the level at which the DBMS describes 'what data are stored and the relationships among them' is the:
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The conceptual (logical) level describes what data exist; the internal level describes how they are stored.

questions.question: Which layer interacts directly with the operating system's file manager and the disk?
questions.subject: Three-Schema Architecture
questions.explanation: The internal level deals with stored records and files on secondary storage.

questions.question: Data independence is defined as:

options.A: The capacity to change the schema at one level without having to change the schema at the next higher level
options.B: Independence of the DBMS from the operating system
options.C: The ability to store data without a DBMS
options.D: The ability of users to work offline

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Data independence follows from the three-schema architecture: only the mapping between two levels needs changing.

questions.question: Logical data independence is the capacity to change the:

options.A: Internal schema without changing the conceptual schema
options.C: Conceptual schema without changing external schemas or application programs
options.D: External schema without changing the conceptual schema

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Changes such as adding a record type or attribute should not affect users whose views do not use them.

questions.question: Physical data independence is the capacity to change the:

options.A: Conceptual schema without changing external schemas
options.C: Application programs without changing the DBMS
options.D: Internal schema without changing the conceptual schema

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Reorganising files or adding access paths should not require changes to the conceptual (and hence external) schemas.

questions.question: Which type of data independence is generally harder to achieve?
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Application programs depend heavily on the logical structure of the data they access, so logical changes are harder to hide.

questions.question: Creating a new index on the ORDERS table to speed up queries requires which kind of data independence to avoid changing programs?
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: An index is an internal-level change.

questions.question: Changing a file organisation from heap to hashed, without affecting queries, is an example of:

options.D: Schema evolution at the external level

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: The storage structure is part of the internal schema.

questions.question: Adding a new attribute Email to the STUDENT relation without affecting existing applications is an example of:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: It changes the conceptual schema; existing views and programs that do not use Email need no change.

questions.question: Splitting the relation EMPLOYEE into two relations and defining a view that reconstructs the original EMPLOYEE for old programs relies on:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema changed, but the view (external schema) hides the change from applications.

questions.question: Moving the database files to a faster SSD without changing any table definitions is an example of:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Only physical storage changed.

questions.question: Data independence in the three-schema architecture is achieved mainly through:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: When a lower-level schema changes, only the mapping to the higher level is updated.

questions.question: In traditional file-processing systems, why is there little data independence?

options.A: Files are stored on tape only
options.D: The structure of data files is embedded in the application programs

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: A change in record format requires changes to every program that uses the file (program–data dependence).

questions.question: In object-oriented databases, 'program–operation independence' means that:

options.B: Every program has its own data
options.C: The implementation of an operation can change without affecting the programs that invoke it

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Users call an operation through its interface (signature); the method body is hidden (encapsulation).

questions.question: Which change requires logical data independence to avoid rewriting application programs?

options.A: Removing an attribute that some views do not use

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Removing an attribute changes the conceptual schema; it affects only views/programs that use it.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Physical data independence implies that external schemas are also unaffected by internal changes.
II. Logical data independence is usually easier to achieve than physical data independence.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: If the conceptual schema is unchanged, the external schemas are unaffected too. Statement II is false: logical independence is harder.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In relational DBMSs, views help to provide logical data independence.
Reason (R): A view can present the old structure of data even after the underlying base tables have been restructured.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Redefining the view over the new tables lets old programs keep working unchanged.

questions.question: Why was physical data independence difficult in older network and hierarchical systems?

options.A: They did not allow data sharing
options.B: Physical pointers and access paths were visible to and used by application programs

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Navigational programs followed pointers explicitly, so storage changes affected the programs.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a change at the internal level?

options.A: Changing the data type of an attribute in the conceptual schema
options.B: Defining a new view for managers
options.C: Creating a clustered index on Emp_id

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Clustered indexes are storage structures, i.e. internal level.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a change at the conceptual level?

options.A: Changing the RAID level of the disks
options.D: Adding a new relationship WORKS_ON between EMPLOYEE and PROJECT

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: New relationships change the logical structure of the whole database.

questions.question: With physical data independence, when the internal schema changes, what must be changed?
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Only the mapping is updated so the conceptual schema continues to describe the same data.

questions.question: With logical data independence, when the conceptual schema changes, what must be changed?

options.B: Only the view definitions and external/conceptual mappings (where affected)

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Application programs referring to external schemas continue to work.

questions.question: Data independence is valuable mainly because it:

options.B: Reduces the maintenance effort when the database structure or storage changes
options.D: Eliminates the need for a DBA

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Programs are insulated from many changes, reducing costly rewrites.

questions.question: Changing the order in which records are physically stored, while SQL queries remain unchanged, is possible because of:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Physical record ordering is an internal-level detail.

questions.question: A DBA merges two tables DEPT_A and DEPT_B into one DEPARTMENT table and provides views with the old names. This is an application of:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema changed, and views keep the external schemas unchanged.

questions.question: The overhead of data independence mainly arises from:

options.A: Mapping requests and results between the levels at run time or compile time

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: More levels and mappings mean more work for the DBMS when processing requests.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT depend on data independence?

options.A: Adding an index without changing programs
options.B: Changing storage devices without changing programs
options.D: Enforcing that each tuple has a unique primary key

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Key constraints are about integrity, not about insulating levels from changes.

questions.question: In the three-schema architecture, physical data independence exists between the:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: It is provided by the conceptual/internal mapping.

questions.question: In the three-schema architecture, logical data independence exists between the:
questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: It is provided by the external/conceptual mappings.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE?

options.A: Data independence means data can never be changed
options.B: File systems provide full data independence
options.C: Logical data independence is guaranteed for every schema change
options.D: Most modern relational DBMSs provide physical data independence well; logical independence is provided mainly through views

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Not every conceptual change can be hidden (e.g. dropping an attribute a view uses), but views handle many cases.

questions.question: A program uses the view EMP_PUBLIC(Name, Dept). The base table EMPLOYEE is split into two tables and the view is redefined. The program needs:

options.C: To be recompiled with new table names

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Because the view name and structure are unchanged, the program continues to work (logical data independence).

questions.question: Adding more RAM to the database server to increase the buffer pool size affects which level, if any, of the three-schema architecture?

options.C: Only the internal/physical implementation, not the schemas seen by users

questions.subject: Data Independence
questions.explanation: Buffer and hardware tuning are physical concerns invisible to the conceptual and external levels.

questions.question: Which language is used by the DBA and database designers to define the conceptual schema?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The DDL compiler processes schema definitions and stores them in the catalog.

questions.question: In a DBMS with a strict separation of levels, the language used to specify the internal schema is the:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The SDL specifies internal (physical) storage; in most relational DBMSs this is done through parameters and commands rather than a separate language.

questions.question: The language used to specify user views and their mappings to the conceptual schema is the:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: In relational DBMSs, SQL itself serves as the VDL (CREATE VIEW).

questions.question: A high-level (non-procedural) DML such as SQL is also described as:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Users specify what data they want, not how to retrieve it; one statement can process many records.

questions.question: A low-level (procedural) DML is typically:

options.B: Record-at-a-time and embedded in a general-purpose programming language

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Procedural DMLs retrieve individual records and need loops and pointers, e.g. DL/I in IMS.

questions.question: When DML statements are embedded in a general-purpose language such as C or Java, the general-purpose language is called the:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The DML is then the data sublanguage.

questions.question: A high-level DML used on its own in an interactive manner is called a:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: SQL used interactively (e.g. at a command prompt) is a query language.

questions.question: Which of the following SQL commands is a DDL command?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: CREATE, ALTER and DROP are DDL; SELECT/INSERT are DML; GRANT is DCL.

questions.question: GRANT and REVOKE belong to which category of SQL commands?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: DCL commands control access privileges.

questions.question: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT belong to which category of SQL commands?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: They control the outcome of transactions.

questions.question: Which statement about DELETE and TRUNCATE is correct?

options.B: DELETE is DML and can use a WHERE clause; TRUNCATE (usually treated as DDL) removes all rows
options.C: TRUNCATE can remove selected rows using WHERE

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: DELETE removes chosen rows row by row; TRUNCATE quickly empties the whole table; DROP removes the table itself.

questions.question: Which SQL statement removes both the data and the definition of a table?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: DROP deletes the schema element itself.

questions.question: The DBMS component that extracts DML commands from an application program written in a host language is the:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The precompiler sends the extracted DML to the DML compiler; the rest goes to the host-language compiler.

questions.question: In embedded SQL, the problem caused by SQL returning sets of rows while the host language processes one record at a time is called:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Cursors bridge the gap by letting the program fetch the result set one row at a time.

questions.question: In embedded SQL, which construct is used to process a multi-row query result one row at a time?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: DECLARE CURSOR, OPEN, FETCH and CLOSE iterate over query results.

questions.question: ODBC and JDBC are examples of:

options.C: Call-level interfaces (APIs) through which programs access databases

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Instead of precompiling embedded SQL, programs call library functions to send SQL to the DBMS.

questions.question: Bank tellers who repeatedly perform a few operations using a small set of commands or function keys are called:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Parametric users run 'canned transactions' through simple interfaces designed for them.

questions.question: A DBMS interface that lets users choose options from lists step by step, without knowing any query language, is a:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Menu-based interfaces, often used for browsing, guide users through options.

questions.question: An interface in which the user fills in the fields of a displayed template to insert or retrieve data is a:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Forms-based interfaces are common for data entry by naive users.

questions.question: A natural language interface to a database:

options.B: Accepts requests written in English (or another natural language) and tries to interpret them
options.C: Is used only by the DBA

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: It uses its own schema of words and a dictionary to interpret requests and generate queries.

questions.question: Privileged commands such as creating accounts, setting system parameters and changing schemas are available through:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: DBA interfaces allow commands that only DBA staff may use.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a DML operation?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Defining relations is a DDL function.

questions.question: In a relational DBMS such as Oracle or MySQL, which statement is TRUE?

options.A: Separate DDL, VDL and SDL languages are always used
options.B: SQL combines the roles of DDL, VDL and DML, and storage details are set through DBA commands and parameters
options.C: Only a record-at-a-time DML is available

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: SQL is a comprehensive language covering data definition, views, manipulation, constraints and access control.

questions.question: The DBMS component that processes schema definitions and stores their descriptions in the catalog is the:
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The catalog then provides the information needed by other modules.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A non-procedural DML specifies what data to retrieve rather than how to retrieve it.
II. A procedural DML requires the programmer to use loops to retrieve multiple records.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Both describe the difference between declarative (SQL) and navigational DMLs.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): SQL is called a declarative language.
Reason (R): In SQL the user specifies the conditions the result must satisfy, and the DBMS decides the access strategy.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The query optimiser chooses the execution plan, so the user need not describe how to retrieve data.

questions.question: Which type of user typically writes complex queries directly in SQL to analyse data, without a canned application?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: Sophisticated users know the DBMS facilities well and write their own requests.

questions.question: Keyword-based database search, similar to web search engines, is an interface where users:

options.C: Type keywords and receive ranked results without writing structured queries

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: It relies on information-retrieval techniques to match keywords with stored data.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of the runtime database processor?

options.A: It provides the graphical user interface
options.B: It executes privileged commands, compiled queries and canned transactions, working with the stored data manager

questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: The runtime processor carries out execution plans and accesses the database through the stored data manager.

questions.question: Which SQL command changes existing values in rows?
questions.subject: Database Languages and Interfaces
questions.explanation: UPDATE is DML and changes data; ALTER is DDL and changes the structure.

questions.question: In a centralised DBMS architecture:

options.A: DBMS functions, application programs and the user interface all run on one central computer, with users connected through terminals
options.B: Each user has a separate copy of the database
options.C: Data is spread across many sites
options.D: Only web browsers can access the data

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Early systems used mainframes with display terminals that had no processing power of their own.

questions.question: A major disadvantage of a purely centralised database system is that:

options.A: It needs a network between sites
options.D: The central computer is a single point of failure and a performance bottleneck

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: If the central machine fails or becomes overloaded, all users are affected.

questions.question: In the basic client/server architecture, a 'server' is:

options.A: Any machine used by an end user
options.B: A system with hardware and software that provides services, such as files, printing, web pages or database access, to clients

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Specialised servers provide functionality to client machines over a network.

questions.question: In a two-tier client/server DBMS architecture, the user interface and application programs usually run on the:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: The client side handles the interface and application logic; the server side handles query and transaction processing.

questions.question: In a two-tier architecture, the database server is often called a:

options.A: Query server or transaction server (an SQL server in relational systems)

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: The server provides query and transaction functionality related to SQL processing.

questions.question: A client program in a two-tier architecture typically connects to the DBMS through a standard API such as:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: ODBC and JDBC let client programs call a DBMS as long as both sides have the necessary software.

questions.question: In the three-tier (web) architecture, the middle tier is the:

options.A: Application server or web server that runs business logic and accesses the database

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: The middle tier stores business rules, checks client credentials and forwards requests to the database server.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of the three-tier architecture over the two-tier architecture?

options.B: Better security, since clients never access the database server directly, and easier scaling
options.D: Business logic must be installed on every client

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: The application server acts as a gatekeeper and business logic is maintained centrally.

questions.question: A 'thin client' is one that:

options.B: Mainly handles presentation, while most processing happens on servers
options.C: Performs most of the processing itself

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Web browsers in three-tier systems are typical thin clients.

questions.question: In a typical two-tier architecture with business logic on the client, the client is often described as a:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Fat clients run substantial application logic and need more software installed.

questions.question: An n-tier architecture:

options.B: Divides the layers between user and stored data further, e.g. separating business logic into several tiers
options.C: Is the same as a centralised architecture

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Additional tiers can be distributed across servers, for example in ERP and enterprise systems.

questions.question: In the three-tier architecture, the correct flow of a request is:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Results travel back the same way, formatted by the middle tier (e.g. as HTML) for the client.

questions.question: Dumb terminals in early centralised systems:

options.D: Provided only display and input, with all processing done on the central computer

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: They were simply screens and keyboards connected to the mainframe.

questions.question: Why did DBMS architectures move from centralised to client/server designs?

options.C: Falling hardware costs let PCs and workstations take over interface and processing work

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Powerful, cheap client machines allowed processing to be moved away from the central computer.

questions.question: Which of the following is typically handled by the database server in a two-tier architecture?

options.A: Query optimisation, transaction management, concurrency control and recovery
options.D: Printing reports on the client's printer

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: These core DBMS functions stay on the server.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In a three-tier architecture, the application server can check a client's credentials before forwarding requests.
II. In a three-tier architecture, business rules must be installed on every client.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Business rules live on the middle tier, which is one of its main advantages.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In a three-tier architecture, changing a business rule usually requires no change on client machines.
Reason (R): Business logic resides in the middle tier rather than on the clients.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Updating the application server updates the logic for all clients at once.

questions.question: A web-based online banking system in which customers use a browser, a bank application server applies business rules and an Oracle server stores data is an example of:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Browser (presentation), application server (business logic) and database server (data) form three tiers.

questions.question: To protect sensitive data travelling between tiers over a network, three-tier systems commonly use:

options.A: Encryption and decryption of transmitted data (e.g. TLS/SSL)

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Encrypting data at the sender and decrypting it at the receiver protects it in transit.

questions.question: In client/server terminology, 'middleware' refers to:

options.B: Software that connects clients to servers and manages communication between them (e.g. ODBC drivers, application servers)
options.C: The hard disk in the middle of the server rack

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Middleware sits between client applications and back-end services.

questions.question: In a two-tier architecture using ODBC, which component must be present on the client side?

options.D: The ODBC driver/client library for the target DBMS

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: The client-side driver translates API calls into requests the DBMS server understands.

questions.question: Which statement about centralised versus client/server architectures is correct?

options.B: Client/server systems always use dumb terminals
options.C: In client/server systems, processing is divided between client and server machines

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Dividing functions between clients and servers is the essence of client/server design.

questions.question: In a client/server DBMS, which of the following is most likely performed on the client in a two-tier design?

options.D: Validating form input and displaying query results

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Presentation and input handling are client-side tasks.

questions.question: In some object DBMS client/server designs, the server supplies disk pages or objects and the client performs much of the processing. Such a server is called a:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: In the data-server approach, more DBMS functionality moves to the client; the server manages storage.

questions.question: Which of these is a specialised server commonly found in client/server environments?
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Client/server systems include file, print, web, e-mail and database servers.

questions.question: A key benefit of client/server DBMS architecture over file sharing on a network is that:

options.A: Whole files must be transferred to each client
options.B: Only the query and its results travel over the network, reducing network traffic
options.C: Clients need a copy of the DBMS

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Processing happens on the server, so only the relevant results are sent to the client.

questions.question: In a web-based three-tier application, the component that generates HTML pages from query results is usually the:
questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: The middle tier formats data (e.g. as HTML or JSON) before sending it to the client.

questions.question: Scalability in a three-tier architecture is improved because:

options.B: Application servers can be replicated and load-balanced independently of the database server
options.D: The database server does all the work

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: Each tier can be scaled separately, e.g. by adding more application servers.

questions.question: A distributed DBMS differs from a client/server DBMS mainly in that:

options.C: The database itself is spread across several sites connected by a network

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: In client/server systems the data usually reside on one server; in a distributed DBMS the data are stored at multiple sites.

questions.question: Which statement about a two-tier architecture is TRUE?

options.B: It always uses a web browser as the client
options.C: The client communicates directly with the database server
options.D: The client never communicates with the DBMS

questions.subject: Centralized and Client/Server Architectures
questions.explanation: In two-tier systems the client talks to the DBMS server directly, typically via ODBC/JDBC.
